o: We must map a (day, month, year) triple in the range 1971–2100 to a weekday name. The key observation is that the calendar repeats with a fixed pattern of leap years, so counting days from a known reference date and taking modulo 7 gives the answer. For example, for day=31, month=8, year=2019: count days from Jan 1, 1971 (a Friday) to Aug 31, 2019; the total number of days elapsed mod 7 tells us how many weekdays to advance from Friday. Since years are bounded by 1971–2100, even a naive day-by-day simulation is at most ~47,000 iterations — trivially fast. Constraints guarantee valid dates, so no validation is needed.
k: Counting days elapsed since a known reference date and reducing mod 7 yields the weekday.
Leap years occur every 4 years except century years not divisible by 400; within 1971–2100 only 2000 is a divisible-by-400 century year.
The problem is small enough that brute-force day-by-day simulation is acceptable, but closed-form counting is cleaner.

a.i: Start from January 1, 1971 (Friday) and advance one day at a time until reaching the target date, cycling through weekday names. This directly mirrors how a human would count on a calendar and needs no date arithmetic tricks. With at most ~47,000 days in range, it easily fits any time limit.
s: Initialize current date as Jan 1, 1971 with weekday index 5 (Friday) in a Sunday-indexed array.
While the current date is not the target, increment the day; if it exceeds the month length, roll over to the next month/year using a leap-year check.
Advance the weekday index cyclically each step.
Return the weekday name at the target index.
a.t: O(D) where D is the number of days between Jan 1, 1971 and the target — at most ~47,000 iterations.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few counters and a constant-size name array.

a.i: Instead of simulating day by day, compute the total number of days from Jan 1, 1971 to the target in O(1): full years contribute 365 or 366 days depending on leap status, months before the target month contribute their fixed lengths plus a leap-day adjustment, then add the day offset. Taking this total mod 7 and offsetting from Friday gives the weekday instantly.
s: Define a leap-year predicate: divisible by 4, excluding centuries unless divisible by 400.
Sum days for complete years 1971..year-1: add 366 per leap year, else 365 (equivalently 365*(y-1971) + count of leaps).
Add cumulative lengths of months 1..month-1 in the target year, plus 1 if month > 2 and the year is a leap year.
Add day - 1 to get total days elapsed since Jan 1, 1971.
Return names[(total + 4) % 7], since Jan 1, 1971 was Friday (index 4 in a Monday=0 scheme, or adjust to your indexing).
a.t: O(Y) where Y ≤ 130 years summed in the loop — effectively O(1); can be made strictly O(1) with a leap-count formula.

a.n: Approach 3: Zeller's congruence / built-in date library
a.i: Zeller's congruence is a classic closed-form formula computing the weekday directly from day, month, and year with pure arithmetic — no reference date needed. Alternatively, most languages offer standard date libraries (e.g., Python's datetime, Java's LocalDate) whose weekday function solves this in one line, which is worth mentioning in an interview as the pragmatic real-world solution.
s: Treat January and February as months 13 and 14 of the previous year.
Compute h = (q + floor(13(m+1)/5) + K + floor(K/4) + floor(J/4) + 5J) mod 7, where q = day, K = year%100, J = year/100.
Map h (0 = Saturday) to the required output strings.
a.t: O(1) — a handful of arithmetic operations (or one library call).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 2 (closed-form counting from the reference date) — it shows you understand modular arithmetic and calendars while remaining simple to verify against the given anchor (Jan 1, 1971 = Friday). Mention Approach 3's library solution as the pragmatic production choice, and know Zeller's congruence by name as a bonus. Common pitfalls: forgetting the leap-day adjustment when month > 2, mishandling century rules (2000 is a leap year, 1900/2100 are not — though 2100 is out of range), and off-by-one errors in the final mod-7 offset (verify with the provided examples before submitting). Edge cases: Jan 1, 1971 itself (zero elapsed days → Friday) and Feb 29 of leap years like 2000. Likely follow-ups: extend to dates outside 1971–2100 (use proleptic Gregorian formulas), compute the number of weekdays between two dates, or handle other calendar systems.
